Demand: Chapter two. Demand, one buyer at a time.

Start with one buyer. This is Ana, from the island's new village; she fishes, and sells her catch at the market. Ask her what a cup of coffee a day is worth to her, and the answer depends on how many she has already had. Her first cup is worth four dollars to her. Her second, two fifty. Her third, one twenty, and a fourth only forty cents. Each cup is worth less than the one before. That's the margin again, the same falling curve as the water. Now suppose coffee costs a dollar fifty a cup. Ana buys a cup whenever it's worth more to her than the price. That's two cups; the third isn't worth a dollar fifty to her. Draw her values as steps, and you have her demand curve: at each price, read across to the step, and down to how many cups she buys.

Now three drinkers. Ana, as before; Bo, who values his first cup at three dollars and his second at one fifty; and Chidi, who'll pay five for his first and two for his second. To get the market's demand, take every cup that anyone wants, and line them up from the most valued to the least. Economists say you add the demands sideways: at each price, count the cups. The result is another staircase, with more and smaller steps. At a dollar fifty, the three of them buy 6 cups between them.

With three drinkers the steps are big. Give the market ten buyers, each with a value drawn at random between nothing and six dollars, and draw how many would buy at each price, as a share of all of them. With a hundred buyers the steps shrink. With a thousand, and then ten thousand, the staircase is a smooth line. That's why textbooks draw demand as a curve: it's a staircase with too many steps to see. When the values are spread evenly, as these are, the line is straight, and it hits zero at six dollars, the price nobody will pay.

That gives the law of demand, and both of its reasons. At a lower price, more people's values clear the bar, so more buyers come in. And each buyer goes further down her own staircase: another cup becomes worth buying. Everything else that matters to a buyer, her income, her tastes, the prices of tea and milk, moves the whole curve, and Parts five and six build it from choices. There are exceptions, goods people buy more of when they get dearer, and Part six finds one in the data, among poor households buying rice in China. They are rare, and they need a special kind of poverty.
Supply: Chapter three. Supply, and the scissors.

Supply is built the same way, from the other side of the market. Here is a coffee farm, and the cost of picking and drying one more sack this week. The first sacks are cheap: the best trees, near the road. Then the hillside, and more pickers to hire. The last sacks need overtime, and the worst land on the farm. Each sack costs more than the one before. That's marginal cost, and it usually rises. If coffee fetches two dollars a sack, the farm sells every sack that costs less than that: 3 of them. Draw the costs as steps and you have the farm's supply curve, rising. Add up every farm sideways, as we added the drinkers, and you have the market's supply.

In 1890 Alfred Marshall, at Cambridge, put the two halves together in the book that taught economics to the world for the next fifty years. The cost of production principle and the final utility principle, he wrote, are both parts of the one law of supply and demand; each may be compared to one blade of a pair of scissors. In later editions he put it more sharply. We might as reasonably dispute whether it is the upper or the under blade of a pair of scissors that cuts a piece of paper, as whether value is governed by utility or cost of production.

Now go back to the pit from Part one, with its twenty cards, and ask which of them set the price. The curves cross at six units. Four cards decide where. The sixth buyer, whose card says 2 dollars 30, and the sixth seller, at 2 dollars 20, are the last ones in: they trade, but only just. The seventh buyer, at 2 dollars 10, and the seventh seller, at 2 dollars 40, are the first ones out. The price has to keep the last ones in and the first ones out, and that pins it between 2 dollars 20 and 2 dollars 30. Every other card could change a great deal without moving it. Let the keenest buyer's card rise as high as you like, or the cheapest seller's cost fall to a dollar: they still trade, and the band doesn't move. The price is set at the margin, by the traders who are only just in and only just out.

So here is the answer to the question of the part, in one picture. A price is where what one more unit is worth to the last buyer meets what one more unit costs the last seller. Neither blade cuts alone. Water is cheap because the last litre costs little to bring to you and is worth little when it arrives. Diamonds are dear because the next carat is costly to find and still badly wanted. Smith's paradox was a paradox only for as long as people looked at the whole instead of the margin.
PlayIt: Chapter four. Play it: guess the price.

Smith didn't trust his first result. I thought perhaps, he wrote, that it was an accident of symmetry in the buyer and seller surpluses. In Part one's pit, the buyers' staircase and the sellers' were close to mirror images, and the price landed in the middle. Maybe that's all convergence was: a market that happened to be balanced. So he ran a lopsided one, where the sellers stood to gain far more than the buyers. Let's run one too. This time you're the economist: you get to see everyone's card.

Here are the cards. The ten buyers are all much alike: the keenest will pay up to two sixty, the least keen two fifteen. The sellers are spread out: the cheapest can sell for sixty cents, the dearest needs two eighty-five. The rules are the pit's rules: anyone may call out a bid or an offer, each trader trades once, and the market opens six times. Before it opens, make your guess. Where will the price settle? Pause if you like.
Two guesses are tempting. The middle of the range of cards, which is 1 dollar 73. Or the average of all twenty cards, 2 dollars 05. Both feel fair. Neither is where this market goes.

Turn the cards into staircases. The buyers' staircase is nearly flat, because the buyers are so alike. The sellers' climbs steeply. They cross at 7 units, and the band of prices that clears the market runs from 2 dollars 25 to 2 dollars 30: right up against the buyers' cards. At that price the buyers keep only 1 dollar 23 between them, and the sellers keep 6 dollars 47. Why so lopsided? Because there are more buyers willing to pay about two twenty-five than there are sellers who can sell at that price, and a buyer who holds out for less is simply replaced by one who won't. The competition is on the buyers' side, so the gains go to the sellers.

Now let the traders loose. These are Agora's learning traders from Part one, who know only their own cards. In the first period most deals are struck at about 2 dollars 07, well below the band: the buyers' bids start low, and the cheap sellers take them. By the third period the deals are in or near the band, and they stay there. Smith's coefficient of convergence falls from 8 percent to under 3. So the lopsided market finds its price too, near the top of the buyers' cards, where the theory put it. That's what Smith found with his students. But notice the grey line. Traders with no intelligence, who found the price in Part one's balanced pit, settle here around 2 dollars 10, well below the band. In a lopsided market, zero intelligence isn't enough. The next chapter is about why.
Converge: Why does a market find the band at all? Go back to Part one's balanced pit. Suppose deals were being struck at 2 dollars 75. At that price 8 sellers would like to sell, but only 3 buyers want to buy. Some seller is left holding a unit, and the price is well above her cost. If she offers a little less, she makes a sale and still gains. So the offers come down. Now suppose deals were at 1 dollar 85. Then 8 buyers want to buy and only 4 sellers will sell, and an unserved buyer can bid a little more and still gain. So the bids go up. Only inside the band can nobody gain by changing what they call out. Economists call that an equilibrium: a state in which no one has a reason to move.

In Part one we met traders with no intelligence at all, the creation of Dhananjay Gode and Shyam Sunder in 1993. Each one calls out a random price that can't lose it money, and none of them learns anything. In the balanced pit, their prices settled close to the band, and they made almost all of the possible gains. It looked as if the rules of the market did nearly all the work. In 1997 Dave Cliff and Janet Bruten, at Hewlett-Packard's laboratories, asked Smith's question about them: was that an accident of symmetry? Here is the test, run in Agora on four markets. In the three lopsided ones, the random traders miss: by 17 cents when the sellers' surplus is large, by 25 cents when supply is flat, by 24 cents when demand is. The traders who learn are within 2 cents of the band in every one. Cliff and Bruten's title said it: zero is not enough.

Why do random traders miss? Look at the market where every seller's cost is two dollars. A random seller asks for any price between two dollars and the top of the range, five. A random buyer bids anything below her card. Deals happen when a high bid meets a low ask, and they average about 2 dollars 25. That number comes from how widely the cards are spread, not from where the curves cross. A trader who learns does what the random one can't: when her offer goes unanswered, she lowers it. With ten sellers all able to sell at two dollars, the price falls to 2 dollars 01, their cost, where the theory says it must. So the rules of the double auction give a market most of its efficiency, as Gode and Sunder said. The price itself needs traders who respond to what they see.

So we can score the prediction from the start of the part. In January 1956 Vernon Smith expected the competitive model to fail. It predicted the price and the quantity of his first market, and of the lopsided one he ran to check. The verdict is wrong, and it's the most productive wrong prediction in this series. It started experimental economics, and won Smith a Nobel prize in 2002.

And the first of the Facts gets its columns. Double auctions converge to the competitive price within a few rounds. Smith's students did it. Agora's learning traders do it by the third period, in every market we tried. Traders with no intelligence do it only when the market is balanced. So Agora agrees with the Fact, and we know which part of Agora is doing the agreeing.
Elasticity: A demand curve says that people buy less when a price rises. Elasticity says how much less. It's the percentage change in the quantity bought, divided by the percentage change in the price that caused it. Percentages, so that it doesn't matter whether you count in litres or gallons, dollars or yen. Through the same point you can draw a steep demand curve or a flat one. Raise the price ten percent. For something people can't easily do without, insulin, or petrol this month, purchases might fall two percent: an elasticity of minus point two. For one brand of cereal on a shelf full of others, they might fall thirty percent: minus three. Below one in size, demand is called inelastic; above one, elastic.

Elasticity isn't the slope of a curve, and it changes as you move along one. Here is the planted demand line of the Island's fish market. Near the top, at five dollars and more, few fish are bought, so a small price cut is a big percentage gain in sales: demand is elastic. Slide down the line and the elasticity falls in size, though the slope never changes. The shaded rectangle is the price times the quantity: what buyers spend, and what sellers take in. While demand is elastic, cutting the price raises spending. At 3 dollars, halfway down, the elasticity is exactly minus one, and spending is as large as it gets. Below that, demand is inelastic, and every cut in price takes in less. That's why a seller with any choice over his price never sets it where demand is inelastic, a fact Part ten will put to work.

In practice you rarely have a curve. You have two points, and the answer depends on which you start from. On the Island, storms keep a third of the boats ashore. On calm days the market sells about 212 fish at 2 dollars 84; on stormy days, 170 at 3 dollars 53. Going from calm to storm, quantity falls 20 percent and the price rises 24 percent: an elasticity of minus 0.82. Going back, from storm to calm, the same two points give minus 1.26. The fix is to measure each change against the average of the two points. This midpoint formula gives minus 1.02 in both directions. And on the Island we can check it against the truth. Along this stretch of the planted line the elasticity runs from about minus point nine to minus one point four, and the midpoint number sits inside that range. Notice what made this work: the storms moved supply, and the price slid along demand. Part four is about when that trick is safe.

Elasticities grow with time. In 2012 three economists in Prague, Tomas Havranek, Zuzana Irsova and Karel Janda, pooled the published estimates for petrol. Corrected for a bias in which estimates get published, the average short-run elasticity was minus 0.09, close to nothing. In the long run it was minus 0.31, more than three times as large. This month you have the same car and the same commute. Over years you can buy a smaller car, move closer to work, or take the bus. They also found that the average published estimate was about twice the corrected one: studies that found a strong response were more likely to be published. Part four is about how that happens, and how to correct for it.
Frost: Chapter seven. Shifts: a frost in Brazil.

Prices move because one of the blades moves. Start where we know the truth: the Island's fish market, over 120 market days. On calm days the boats go out, and the price and the catch settle near the same spot, scattered a little because the villagers' appetites vary from day to day. On stormy days a third of the boats stay ashore. The supply curve swings to the left, and the price rises and the catch falls. The stormy days lie along the planted demand line, because nothing about the buyers changed: the price moved along their curve.

That gives a habit of thought economists use every day. When the price rises and the quantity falls, supply has fallen: a frost, a storm, a new tax on sellers. When the price falls and the quantity rises, supply has risen. When both rise together, demand has risen; when both fall, demand has fallen. It's called comparative statics: move one blade, hold the other still, and compare where the market settles. When both blades move at once, you need more than two points, and that is the subject of Part four.

Now the real world, where nothing is planted. On the night of the eighteenth of July 1975, a black frost, so called because it blackens the leaves, swept across Paraná, in southern Brazil, the state that grew much of Brazil's coffee. According to the United States Department of Agriculture, Brazil's next crop was 60 percent smaller than the one before: from 23.0 million sacks to 9.3 million. Brazil grew about 32 percent of the world's coffee, so the world's crop fell 16 percent. Here is the price of Arabica coffee, month by month, as it was quoted at the time. In June 1975 it was 1 dollar 23 a kilo. The frost hit, and the price climbed for nearly two years, to 7 dollars in April 1977: 5.7 times as much.

What does that tell us? If supply moved and demand stayed put, the price slid along the demand curve, and the two changes give its elasticity. The world's crop fell by about 18 percent, measured from the midpoint, and the average price rose by about 113 percent. That's an elasticity of about minus 0.16: in the short run, coffee drinkers hardly respond at all. Treat that number gently. Warehouses sold coffee picked in earlier years, so less was drunk than the crop alone suggests. Traders bid for the next harvests too. And the long run came: the world's crop recovered by 1978, and the price fell back. That's elasticity growing with time, on the supply side.

Coffee has been through this again and again. Here is the whole history since 1960, in today's dollars. Frosts in the Brazilian winter of 1994 sent the price up by half in a single month, from 3 dollars 16 a kilo in June to 4 dollars 83 in July. In February 2025, after poor Brazilian harvests, Arabica averaged 9 dollars 05 a kilo, the highest monthly price in the World Bank's records, in dollars of the day. But a dollar of 1977 bought far more. In today's money the peak after the black frost was about 39 dollars a kilo, four times the record of 2025. Whenever you compare prices across decades, divide by the price of everything else first.
Surplus: How much good does a market do? The first person to answer properly was a French engineer, Jules Dupuit, in 1844. His question was practical: is a bridge worth building? The obvious answer was to count the tolls it would collect. Dupuit saw that the tolls miss most of it. Line up the travellers by what a crossing is worth to each of them. The tolls are this rectangle. But everyone who crosses would have paid more than the toll, some of them much more, and that difference is a gain that nobody collects. And the travellers the toll turns away, whose crossing would have cost the bridge nothing, lose this triangle. The bridge's real value is all of it. Marshall named the middle area: he called it consumer's rent at first, and then consumer's surplus, the name that stuck.

Dupuit's idea measures any market. Here is Part one's pit again. At a price of 2 dollars 25, each buyer who trades keeps the difference between her card and the price: the blue steps, 3 dollars 40 in all. Each seller keeps the price less his cost: the amber steps, 3 dollars 30. Together that's 6 dollars 70, and no other arrangement of these twenty people can make more. Drop the last pair, and the market loses the thin step between them. Add one more pair, the seventh buyer and the seventh seller, and the unit costs more to make than it's worth to the person who gets it: that loses money too. The competitive quantity is exactly the one that makes the most.

With many traders the steps become areas. On the Island's fish market, the villagers' surplus is this triangle, about 329 dollars a day, and the fishers' is this one, about 247. Now suppose something stops the market at 150 fish a day. Every fish between there and the competitive quantity was worth more to some buyer than it cost some fisher to catch, and none of them is caught. That triangle of gains is simply gone; it doesn't move to anyone. Economists call it a deadweight loss, and Arnold Harberger made a career of measuring it. Taxes and price controls both cut a market off short of its competitive quantity. The next two chapters measure what that costs, and who pays.
Tax: Chapter nine. Who pays a tax?

Put a tax of 40 cents on every unit sold in the pit, and make the sellers pay it. To a seller, the tax is like a higher cost: a seller whose card says two dollars now needs two dollars 40 to break even. The whole supply staircase rises by 40 cents. Run the market with Agora's learning traders. Before the tax, 6 units traded at about 2 dollars 25. Now the buyers pay about 2 dollars 46, and the sellers, after handing over the tax, keep about 2 dollars 06. Each side has lost about twenty cents. And one unit fewer is traded. That unit was worth 10 cents more to its buyer than it cost its seller, and that's the deadweight loss of the tax: the gain from a trade the tax prevented, which nobody gets, not even the government.

Now take the same tax off the sellers and put it on the buyers: at the till, every buyer pays the price plus 40 cents to the government. The price called out in the pit falls, to about 2 dollars 03. But add the tax, and the buyers give up 2 dollars 43, within a few cents of before. The sellers keep 2 dollars 03, also within a few cents. And the same number of units trade. This is one of the most useful results in economics, and one of the least believed. Who hands the money to the government doesn't decide who bears the tax. The market moves the price until the burden falls where it falls, whichever side the law names.

So where does the burden fall? On whichever side can get out of the way less. The share buyers bear is the sellers' elasticity over the sum of the two. On the Island's fish market, buyers respond a little less than fishers do, so buyers bear about 57 percent of a tax on fish. When demand hardly responds, as with cigarettes, or petrol this month, the buyers pay nearly all of it. When supply can't respond at all, the sellers pay. Land is the classic case: there's only so much of it, so a tax on land falls on its owners, which is why Henry George wanted to tax nothing else.

The theory has two quiet assumptions, and the evidence finds both of them failing. The first is that people see the tax. In 2009 Raj Chetty, Adam Looney and Kory Kroft tagged about seven hundred and fifty products in a grocery store with prices that included the sales tax, for three weeks. Sales of those products fell by about eight percent, though the price at the till hadn't changed at all. Taxes that are hidden until the checkout are partly invisible. The second is that the tax is paid. American states collect their diesel taxes at different points: some from the retailer, some from the supplier further up the chain. Wojciech Kopczuk and his co-authors found that more of the tax reaches the pump price when suppliers remit it, because retailers evade more. So who writes the cheque matters exactly when it changes who notices the tax, or who manages not to pay it.
Controls: Now let the law set a price. Back in the pit, suppose no unit may sell for more than 2 dollars, below the band. At that price only the sellers whose costs are 2 dollars or less will sell: 5 of them. But 7 buyers want to buy. There's a shortage of 2. The price can't do its job of deciding who gets the scarce units, so something else has to. The question is what.

There are two answers on paper. If the five units went to the five keenest buyers, the market would lose only the triangle, one unit's worth, and still make 98.5 percent of what it could. If they went by lottery among everyone who wants one, some would go to buyers who value them least, and the market would make only 83 percent. Run the pit, and Agora's learning traders make 84 percent: the lottery, almost exactly. Under the cap every buyer soon bids the maximum, so a unit goes to whoever calls first, whatever his card. That's the hidden cost of a price control. The triangle is only part of it; the rest is that the goods end up with the wrong people. Edward Glaeser and Erzo Luttmer found it in New York's rent-controlled flats: compared with cities without rent control, a sizeable share of apartments housed the wrong kinds of households.

In the real world the commonest answer is a queue. In 1973 and 74, and again in 1979, the United States held the price of petrol below what the market would have set, and drivers waited at the pumps for hours; some states let cars fill up only on odd or even days. A queue is a price too, paid in time instead of money, and nobody receives it. And it hands the goods to whoever's time is cheapest, which is not the same as whoever values them most. In 1980 a court order held down the price at Chevron's stations in California, and Robert Deacon and Jon Sonstelie used the queues that formed to measure what drivers' time was worth to them.

The best evidence on a modern price control comes from San Francisco. In 1994 the city extended rent control to small apartment buildings built before 1980, and left those built later uncontrolled, which gave Rebecca Diamond, Tim McQuade and Franklin Qian a comparison. Rent control did what it was meant to do for sitting tenants: they were about twenty percent less likely to move, and fewer were pushed out of the city. But landlords of the controlled buildings cut the rental housing they offered by fifteen percent, by selling to owner-occupiers and redeveloping. Less rental housing means higher rents for everyone looking for a flat, and the authors concluded that this probably undid much of what the law set out to achieve.

A floor is the mirror image. Set a minimum price of 2 dollars 60. Only 4 buyers will pay that much, but 8 sellers would like to sell at it, so the sellers are rationed instead. If the four cheapest sold, the market would keep 91 percent of its gains. By lottery, 67 percent; and Agora's traders make 67. The commonest floor on a price is a minimum wage, and there the evidence is subtler than this pit, because employers may have power over wages to begin with. That's Part thirty-eight.

Notice what the evidence does and doesn't settle. It tells us what a rent cap does: sitting tenants pay less and stay put, and newcomers face fewer flats at higher rents. Whether to have one needs something more: a judgment about how much the security of the people already housed is worth, against the cost to the people still looking, and who should pay for it. Economics can measure both sides of that ledger. It can't, by itself, tell you how to weigh them.
Dials: Chapter twelve. The Dials: how much do people respond?

Every part enters what it has learned into the Dials, the numbers economics runs on, each with its range of estimates and how they were measured. This part fills the first one: the price elasticity of demand for staples. For petrol, the corrected averages we met earlier: minus 0.09 within a year, minus 0.31 in the long run. For cigarettes, a meta-analysis by Craig Gallet and John List averaged minus 0.48 over more than five hundred estimates. For alcohol, Alexander Wagenaar and his co-authors pooled more than a thousand: about minus 0.46 for beer, minus 0.69 for wine and minus 0.80 for spirits. Every one is below one in size. That's why taxes on these goods raise so much revenue: people keep buying. It's also why, as health policy, such taxes work, but slowly, and the long-run numbers matter more than the short.

Here are the first sixteen of the Dials. One is lit. The rest are drawn empty, each with the part that will fill it: the elasticity of intertemporal substitution in Part seven, markups in Part ten, the multipliers of government spending in Part thirty-two. By the end of the series every one of them will have its estimates, its designs, and a verdict on how settled it is.
